extracted.intended_audience: students, researchers, and practitioners interested in philosophy of science, psychology, education, and the scientific study of human character (ethology).
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for scientific investigation of the formation of character (ethology): how to choose methods (deduction vs experiment/observation), what kinds of laws count as scientific, and how to interpret empirical generalizations about human character. Applies to researchers constructing causal explanations of complex mental and social phenomena.

rubrics_metrics.name: Analyse mental states by their causal laws (association)
rubrics_metrics.description: Inquire what beliefs and desires we have by direct consciousness, and according to what laws one belief produces another; examine what objects we desire naturally and by what causes we are made to desire things originally indifferent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The general laws of association prevail among complex states of mind as among simpler ones: desires, emotions, abstract ideas, judgments and volitions, when habitual, are called up by association according to the same laws as simple ideas. Investigations should trace how one state of mind produces another in accordance with these laws.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consider alternatives for differences of mental susceptibility
rubrics_metrics.description: When explaining differences in mental susceptibility among individuals, consider three possible sources: (1) original/ultimate differences, (2) consequences of previous mental history, (3) varieties of physical (organic) organization.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not accept crude generalizations that attribute differences solely to bodily structure; analyze how organic differences may act indirectly (e.g., by making sensations more intense and thereby changing associative outcomes). Avoid accepting empirical experience in the gross without analysis.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguish empirical laws from causal (scientific) laws
rubrics_metrics.description: Empirical laws are uniformities true within observed limits but not guaranteed beyond them; scientific truths are the causal laws that explain empirical generalizations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: An empirical law may be the consequence of prior causes not yet ascertained or may depend on multiple agencies; scientific inquiry should seek the causal laws that explain when and why empirical generalizations hold and what limits them.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prefer deductive (causal) investigation for complex phenomena
rubrics_metrics.description: For highly complex phenomena like the formation of character, the Deductive Method—starting from general laws and verifying their consequences by specific experience—is the appropriate method; direct experimental control is ordinarily impossible.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Experimental investigation would require controlling and recording every sensation and impression from infancy onward, which is practically impossible. Thus deduce the effects of assumed circumstances from general laws of mind (Psychology → Ethology).

rubrics_metrics.name: Use observation only with caution and adequate scope
rubrics_metrics.description: Simple observation and en masse comparisons yield only approximate empirical generalizations and cannot by themselves identify precise causal connections in complex cases.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Observational conclusions deserve no reliance unless instances are numerous enough to eliminate chance and shared peculiarities. It is difficult to ascertain an individual's character reliably from limited actions; comparisons require sufficiently large and accurately selected samples.

rubrics_metrics.name: Verify deductive hypotheses against empirical generalizations
rubrics_metrics.description: When using deduction, verify the results by comparing deductions with empirical laws (general propositions derived from many instances), not merely by single instances.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Before applying high-level laws deductively to a new class of phenomena, go as far as practicable in ascertaining empirical laws so deductions can be compared to general observed propositions (Newton/Kepler example).

rubrics_metrics.name: Formulate ethological propositions as tendencies, not certainties
rubrics_metrics.description: Propositions in Ethology should be hypothetical and assert tendencies (what a cause tends to produce) rather than absolute certainties about what will always happen.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: E.g., bodily strength tends to make men courageous; experience tends to give wisdom. Because multiple agencies may frustrate tendencies, scientific propositions should state limits and conditional tendencies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Choose order of induction flexibly, based on practicable induction
rubrics_metrics.description: There is no unbending maxim that induction must proceed from lowest to middle to highest principles; the order should depend on where conditions for real induction can most completely be realized.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In sciences of cause, often highest/middle principles are best ascertained first (e.g., laws of motion). Obtain those truths first for which induction is most practicable; use empirical laws to verify, not to restrict logical order rigidly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Expect empirical generalizations to be approximate in complex domains
rubrics_metrics.description: Because many modifying circumstances affect human phenomena, empirical laws in psychology and social domains are usually approximate and limited to contexts similar to those of observation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Even astronomy yields approximations (Kepler's laws approximate due to perturbations). Be particularly cautious applying maxims collected in one nation, age, or set of circumstances to another.

rubrics_metrics.name: Trace observed character differences to causal circumstances rather than treat them as ultimate facts
rubrics_metrics.description: When differences in character (e.g., between ages, sexes, or nations) are observed, seek explanations in differing experiences, education, occupations, social position, and physical peculiarities instead of assuming them as unexplainable ultimate facts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: youth/age differences arise largely from differing experiences and inclinations; national character changes with institutions and events. Connecting empirical observations to causal laws justifies greater confidence in both observation and reasoning.

rubrics_metrics.name: Identify and value middle principles (axiomata media)
rubrics_metrics.description: Middle-level principles (those between lowest empirical laws and highest generalizations) are of principal value for explaining phenomena and should be sought and used in scientific explanation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These middle principles can be reached by deduction as corollaries from general laws; their discovery route (deductive or inductive) should be governed by what yields reliable verification and explanatory power.

rubrics_metrics.name: Acknowledge direct organic bases for some mental facts (instincts)
rubrics_metrics.description: Some mental facts—especially instincts—may have a direct and immediate connection with physical conditions of the brain and nerves, even though they can be modified by education and other mental influences.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: No satisfactory psychological-only hypothesis explains instincts; consider physiological investigation while recognizing capacity for modification in humans and some animals.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use knowledge of tendencies pragmatically to shape circumstances
rubrics_metrics.description: Even imperfect causal knowledge that identifies tendencies is practically valuable: when circumstances are controllable, arranging them according to known tendencies can influence character formation toward desired ends.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ethology's role is to indicate tendencies so that shaping education or social conditions can increase the likelihood of desired character outcomes, understanding the limits of such control.
